strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: extending diffusion-based image editing capabilities to high-resolution (1K, 2K+) domains without retraining large foundation models.

The proposed method is technically neat and well-motivated: using a lightweight 1x1 convolution transfer function on intermediate diffusion features via test-time trajectory alignment effectively captures high-frequency texture details.

The patch synchronization mechanism (blended Tweedie updates combined with a reverse/resampling strategy) cleverly prevents seam artifacts without requiring costly overlapping sliding-window diffusion passes or optimizing on auxiliary patches.
The method demonstrates flexibility across different model families, functioning on both U-Net-based architectures (Stable Diffusion v2.1) and DiT-based models (FLUX.1-dev).
weaknesses: Lack of inference time and computational cost analysis: The pipeline requires null-text inversion, patch-wise forward trajectories, per-timestep optimization of 1x1 convolutions for each patch, and reverse sampling with resampling steps. A detailed breakdown of runtime, GPU memory consumption, and throughput compared to baselines is essential.

Evaluation relies solely on low-level fidelity/reconstruction metrics on masked unchanged regions (M-MSE, M-SSIM, M-PSNR, HaarPSI). Metrics measuring text alignment or editing quality (e.g., CLIP score, ImageReward, or a perceptual user study) are missing to confirm that high-frequency detail transfer does not compromise the intended semantic modification.

Baseline comparisons are limited strictly to off-the-shelf super-resolution models chained after low-resolution editing. Comparisons or discussions regarding training-free high-resolution generation/editing frameworks (e.g., adapting FreeScale, ScaleCrafter, or DemoFusion for editing) would provide a stronger evaluation.

Minor inconsistencies in hyperparameters: Section 5.1 states that tau = 15 is set as the default hyperparameter, whereas Appendix Table 2 states that the default setting tau = 35 achieves the best performance across all metrics.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem: extending text-driven image editing capabilities to high resolutions (e.g., 2K) without requiring retraining of large foundation models.

The proposed technical components are well-motivated: using a lightweight 1x1 convolution to adaptively transfer intermediate features between diffusion trajectories, along with a blended Tweedie update and resampling strategy that synchronizes non-overlapping patches without heavy overlapping inference overhead.

The qualitative comparisons in Figures 4, 5, and 7 clearly show that the synchronization mechanism prevents seam artifacts and that the detail enhancement retains high-frequency texture better than naive super-resolution cascading.
The method demonstrates architectural versatility, showing compatibility with both U-Net (Stable Diffusion v2.1) and DiT (FLUX.1-dev) backbones.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparison: Comparing ScaleEdit against off-the-shelf single-image super-resolution (Real-ISR) baselines (DiT-SR, DiT4SR, PiSA-SR, TSD-SR) is inherently asymmetric. Real-ISR models only observe the low-resolution edited image and have zero access to the high-resolution source image (I_src^high). The evaluation should include Reference-based Super-Resolution (Ref-SR) methods or guided restoration baselines that condition on the high-resolution reference.

Lack of semantic editing and prompt alignment metrics: The quantitative evaluation only reports masked pixel/perceptual reconstruction metrics (M-MSE, M-SSIM, M-PSNR, HaarPSI) measuring how well unedited regions match the source. There are no quantitative metrics evaluating semantic adherence to the edit instruction (e.g., CLIP direction similarity, Image-Reward) or user studies assessing whether the high-frequency detail injection interferes with the intended edit.

Evaluation is restricted to synthetic images: The evaluation data consists exclusively of 400 images generated via FreeScale and edited with NanoBanana. Evaluation on diverse real-world high-resolution photography is missing.

Missing runtime and memory analysis: The pipeline relies on test-time optimization per patch and per timestep up to threshold tau, along with multiple forward/reverse diffusion operations. A breakdown of wall-clock latency, GPU memory footprint, and scaling behavior across resolutions (e.g., 1K vs 2K vs 4K) is needed to evaluate practical deployment.

Contradiction in hyperparameter specifications: Section 5.1 specifies the default hyperparameter as tau = 15, whereas Appendix D (Table 2) states that 'the default setting tau = 35 achieves the best performance across all metrics.' This discrepancy should be clarified.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: extending diffusion-based image editing to high resolutions (1K, 2K, and beyond) without requiring end-to-end retraining or fine-tuning of large diffusion models.

The formulation of detail transfer via a lightweight, spatially adaptive 1x1 convolution optimized in intermediate feature space between low-resolution and high-resolution source trajectories is technically neat and intuitive.

The proposed patch synchronization strategy (using blended Tweedie estimates on half-offset auxiliary patches combined with a DDIM resampling step) effectively eliminates boundary artifacts without needing full overlapping patch generation during optimization.
Demonstrates applicability across both U-Net (Stable Diffusion v2.1) and Diffusion Transformer (FLUX.1-dev) backbones.

Quantitative improvements over cascade baselines (low-resolution editing + state-of-the-art super-resolution) on masked preservation metrics (M-PSNR, M-SSIM, M-MSE, HaarPSI) supporting the claim that source high-frequency details are better retained.
weaknesses: No runtime or computational cost analysis is provided. The method relies on test-time optimization (Null-text inversion, per-patch feature optimization over diffusion timesteps up to hyperparameter tau, and auxiliary latent denoising passes). For a 2K image divided into 16 patches (at 512x512 native resolution), the wall-clock time and GPU memory consumption are likely substantial, which is a critical factor for practical usability.

Strong dependency on external low-resolution image editors: The method fundamentally requires a pre-edited low-resolution reference image ($I^{low}_{ref}$). Consequently, the task formulation is closer to detail-preserving reference-guided upsampling/transfer rather than an autonomous high-resolution editing framework. Failures or artifacts from the base editor directly propagate to the output.

Missing evaluation on editing instruction fidelity: The quantitative evaluation focuses exclusively on masked reconstruction of unchanged regions (M-MSE, M-PSNR, M-SSIM) and HaarPSI against the source image. There are no quantitative metrics evaluating prompt-edit alignment (e.g., CLIP text-image score, CLIP directional similarity, or human evaluation) to ensure that detail injection does not degrade the semantic edit intended by the user.

Baseline comparison is narrow: Comparisons are only drawn against combining one low-resolution editor (NanoBanana) with standalone super-resolution models. Relevant high-resolution synthesis frameworks adapted for editing or tuning-free scale adaptation methods (e.g., ScaleCrafter, DemoFusion) are not benchmarked.

Inconsistency in reported hyperparameter defaults: Section 5.1 specifies the default cutoff timestep as $\tau = 15$, whereas Appendix D states that 'the default setting $\tau = 35$ achieves the best performance across all metrics' in Table 2.

strengths: Practical and timely problem: Addressing high-resolution (>1K, up to 8K) image editing by bypassing the fixed native resolution limitations of diffusion/flow models without requiring full retraining is a valuable and relevant direction.

Methodological formulation: Parameterizing the feature transfer function via a 1x1 convolution on intermediate generative features allows spatially adaptive cross-channel mixing, successfully bridging the low-resolution and high-resolution generation trajectories.

Seamless patch synchronization: The blended-Tweedie update combined with the resampling strategy (Sec. 4.5) offers a neat, computationally conscious way to suppress boundary seam artifacts without incurring the full overhead of dense overlapping window inference.

Model generality: The approach is derived and validated across both U-Net DDIM architectures (Stable Diffusion v2.1) and transformer-based Rectified Flow architectures (FLUX.1-dev), showing good flexibility.
weaknesses: High computational latency: As reported in Appendix G, the test-time optimization takes ~235 seconds per 1K image without Null-Text Inversion and ~636 seconds (>10 minutes) with NTI on an NVIDIA A6000. As resolution scales up to 2K (4 patches) and 8K (64+ patches), the cumulative inference time becomes prohibitively heavy for interactive editing workflows.

Reliance on pre-existing low-resolution edits: The formulation fundamentally relies on an already edited low-resolution reference ($I_{ref}^{low}$) produced by an external editor (e.g., Nano Banana). Any semantic inconsistencies, geometric deformations, or hallucinations in the low-resolution reference will inevitably propagate to the final high-resolution output.

Narrow baseline comparison spectrum: The comparative evaluation focuses almost entirely on combining low-resolution editing with diffusion super-resolution baselines (DiT-SR, DiT4SR, PiSA-SR, TSD-SR). While this validates the premise that standard SR neglects high-frequency source conditioning, the paper misses comparisons or discussions against training-free high-resolution generation/editing frameworks adapted for editing (e.g., DemoFusion, ScaleCrafter, or patch-based inpainting approaches).

Potential feature mismatch in heavily edited regions: The transfer function $\phi_\theta$ is optimized to map low-resolution source features to high-resolution source features (Eq. 6), but is then directly applied to the edited reference trajectory (Eq. 9). When an object undergoes drastic semantic replacement (e.g., dragon to plane, or man to monk), transferring source-derived feature offsets risk injecting incongruent high-frequency textures or artifacts onto the newly introduced subject.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: extending image editing to high resolutions (>1K, 2K, up to 8K) without retraining large-scale diffusion models.

The technical design is well-motivated: using a learnable 1x1 convolution transfer function on intermediate feature maps to capture fine-grained source details, and introducing a blended Tweedie update with resampling that mitigates boundary artifacts across patches without redundant overlapping sliding-window inference.
The framework is model-agnostic and demonstrated on both U-Net architectures (Stable Diffusion v2.1) and Flow-Matching DiT architectures (FLUX.1-dev).

Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments against representative diffusion super-resolution pipelines (DiT-SR, DiT4SR, PiSA-SR, TSD-SR) show consistent improvements in detail preservation and mask-level source fidelity on both synthetic and real images.
weaknesses: High computational cost and runtime: Because the framework relies on test-time optimization (and optionally Null-text inversion), inference takes ~235 to 635 seconds per 1K image on an NVIDIA A6000. The runtime scaling for larger resolutions (e.g., 2K, 4K, 8K) involves $N \times M$ patches, which would significantly increase computational latency.

Evaluation metrics in Table 1 and Table 4 focus entirely on reconstruction fidelity and perceptual similarity (HaarPSI, Masked-MSE/SSIM/PSNR, LPIPS) rather than target editing alignment. While Table 3 reports CLIP similarity for an ablation, the main benchmarks lack text-image alignment metrics (e.g., CLIP score / Image-Text matching) or a perceptual user study assessing editing quality.

Baseline comparisons are limited to Edit-then-SR pipelines; comparing or discussing against existing high-resolution generative/editing strategies adapted with tiling or scale-fusion (such as DemoFusion or FreeScale adapted to editing) would provide a stronger empirical perspective.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in generative modeling: extending existing text-guided image editing models beyond their native training resolutions (e.g., 2K, 4K, 8K) without requiring retraining.

The technical design is well-motivated: using a lightweight 1x1 convolution as a learnable intermediate feature transfer function allows spatial adaptivity while preserving structural layout during trajectory alignment.

The proposed patch synchronization mechanism (combining blended Tweedie estimates with forward latent resampling) elegantly avoids the heavy computational burden of overlapping patch-diffusion sliding windows.
Demonstrates versatility across different diffusion architectures, showing successful adaptation to both U-Net (Stable Diffusion v2.1) and Rectified Flow / Transformer (FLUX.1-dev) backbones.

Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets show consistent improvements in detail preservation and boundary consistency compared to standard Edit + Super-Resolution pipelines.
weaknesses: Heavy computational and runtime overhead: As disclosed in the supplementary material, 1K editing requires ~235s (without NTI) to ~635s (with NTI) on an NVIDIA A6000 GPU. Because runtime scales with the number of patches, 2K (4 patches) and 8K (64–256 patches) inference entails substantial execution times. A detailed breakdown and scaling discussion across resolutions is missing.

Baselines are somewhat disadvantaged: The chosen baselines (LR Edit + standalone SR models) do not have access to the high-resolution source image $I_{src}^{high}$, making it natural that they fail on source-detail preservation metrics (e.g., M-SSIM, M-PSNR). Incorporating a simple compositing baseline (e.g., splicing the masked high-res source background with super-resolved edited foreground) or reference-based restoration baselines would provide a more rigorous benchmark.

Absence of human perceptual evaluation: Given the subjective nature of semantic image editing, detail fidelity, and boundary artifacts across patches, a structured user study would significantly strengthen the empirical claims.
